title: At the café — and nouns as objects
goal: Order drinks and snacks with four forms that are always polite — and install the tožilnik (Accusative), the form a noun takes when it is the OBJECT of an action, not the one doing it.
bekal: use two verbs that don't play by the rules: *jesti* (to eat) and *piti* (to drink)

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Tri naročila in en račun
dialogs.intro: Afternoon at a kavarna on the banks of the Ljubljanica. Maja, Eva, and Budi sit outside; the waiter comes over with a notepad.

lines.speaker: Eva:
lines.id: Tea for me. Green tea, please.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: In jaz bi vodo in eno pivo.
lines.id: And I'd like water and a beer.
lines.literal: and I would water-acc and one beer.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Malo, prosim. Imate kaj za pod zob?
lines.id: Small, please. Do you have any snacks?
lines.literal: small, please. you-have something for under tooth?

lines.speaker: Natakar:
lines.id: We have burek, sandwiches, and salad.

lines.speaker: Maja:
lines.id: And just one bill for all of us.

lines.speaker: Natakar:
lines.id: Of course. I'll be right back.

notes: **Jaz bi … — the way you'll hear people order most.** Literally "I would", with the verb deliberately dropped: *Jaz bi eno kavo* is really cut down from *Jaz bi rad eno kavo* ("I would like a coffee"). The short form is polite, warm, and used by Slovenians every day — far more often than *Želim*, which sounds like a form you fill in.

**Kava becomes kavo, voda becomes vodo, solata becomes solato.** This is the tožilnik (Accusative): the form a noun takes when it's the **object** of an action. The rule for feminine words is a single line — swap *-a* for *-o* — and it works on thousands of words.

**But čaj, burek, and sendvič don't change at all.** Masculine nouns that aren't living things use the same form whether they're the subject or the object. So half your worry about cases just evaporated: *Pijem čaj*, *Čaj je vroč* — the forms are twins.

**Zame = za + mene.** The preposition *za* (for) merges with its pronoun: *zame* (for me), *zate* (for you), *zanj* (for him), *zanjo* (for her), *za naju* (for us two). Fused forms like this are common in Slovenian and are always shorter than the long version.

**Kaj za pod zob** is literally "something for under the tooth" — the everyday expression for a snack. Slovenian is full of body images like this, and phrases like these are what make people smile when you use them. **Kar** in *račun kar skupaj* is a softener, like English "just": it makes a request sound relaxed, not demanding.

grammars.title: Tožilnik — the object form
body: Slovenian marks who does what to whom through the **form of the noun**, not through word order. That's why the order can be shuffled without the sentence changing its meaning.
after: Three of the four groups ask nothing of you: masculine words that aren't alive and **all** neuter words keep the same form. The only real work is two things: *-a* → *-o* for feminine words, and an added *-a* for living masculine ones.

The living/non-living split is taken seriously: *Vidim brata* (I see my brother) but *Vidim stol* (I see a chair). Living means people and animals — not plants, and not cars, however much their owners love them.

grammars.title: Four ways to order that are always right
body: Here are the forms, from the most relaxed to the most formal. All are polite; none of them can make you sound rude.
after: The last row is very handy: **še** means "more" or "another". *Še enkrat, prosim* = "once more, please" — a sentence you'll use every day when people talk too fast.
To ask for the bill: *Račun, prosim* or *Plačal bi* (I'd like to pay; a woman says *Plačala bi*). To pay separately: *Vsak zase, prosim* — literally "each for himself".

grammars.title: Jesti in piti — two verbs that don't play by the rules
body: The two verbs used most at the table, and both have forms that follow no pattern. Learn them as chunks.
after: Notice the lovely trap in the third row: **je** means "he/she eats" **and** "he/she is". *Ona je* can mean "she is" or "she eats", and only what follows tells them apart. *Ona je učiteljica* = she's a teacher. *Ona je kruh* = she's eating bread. Slovenians themselves make jokes about it.

The negative of *jesti*: **ne jem** is written as two words but said as one. For "not have", the form is *nimam*, and whatever is missing always takes the Genitive: *Nimam časa* (I don't have time), *Ni piva* (there's no beer).

sections.title: Pijača in prigrizki — drinks and snacks

blocks.text: Every word below is given twice: its basic form, then the form you say when ordering. Learn the second column — that's what comes out of your mouth in a café.

Coffee in Slovenia has its own vocabulary: **bela kava** (white coffee), **kava z mlekom** (coffee with milk), **espresso**, and **makijato**. If you just order *kava*, you'll get a short espresso — not a big mug of filter coffee. For a longer one, ask for *podaljšano kavo*.

**Burek** is a layered pastry filled with meat or cheese, a legacy of the Yugoslav era, and the lifesaver of every Ljubljana student at two in the morning. It's sold by the piece and doesn't change form when you order it — a small gift for the hungry language learner.
A few habits that aren't written in any grammar book, but that people notice right away if you break them.

head: Slovenščina
Say it
When to use
rows: Here you go; here's your order

blocks.text: **Dober tek** is said to anyone who is eating or about to eat — including strangers at the next table. Walking past people eating without a word feels a little cold, just like not saying hello when you step into an elevator.

**Na zdravje!** comes with one rule people take seriously: when you clink glasses, **look the other person in the eye**. Not at the glass — in the eye. Slovenians, like their Austrian and German neighbors, see staring at the glass as a sign of insincerity, and some will even tell you what bad luck follows. The same phrase is also said when someone sneezes.
